q: When choosing a rehabilitation modality for shoulder tendon pain, what distinguishes therapeutic ultrasound from superficial heating and cooling?
o: Electrical energy delivered through skin electrodes to activate a muscle
Acoustic energy absorbed by tissue and converted into heat
Cooling energy producing vasoconstriction in the skin
Thermal energy primarily warming skin and subcutaneous tissue
explanation:
**Therapeutic ultrasound** is a deep-heating modality. Its acoustic energy is absorbed by tissues and converted to heat, unlike superficial heat, cooling, or electrical muscle stimulation (p. 826). "The most popular deep heating modality is ultrasound, a form of acoustic energy, which when absorbed by tissues is converted into heat." (p. 826).

**A. Electrical energy delivered through skin electrodes to activate a muscle.** Wrong, electrically activating muscle describes neuromuscular stimulation, not the acoustic energy used by ultrasound (p. 826).
**B. Acoustic energy absorbed by tissue and converted into heat.** Correct, absorption of acoustic energy and its conversion into heat is the mechanism given for therapeutic ultrasound (p. 826).
**C. Cooling energy producing vasoconstriction in the skin.** Wrong, cutaneous vasoconstriction is an effect of cold therapy, whereas ultrasound is a deep-heating modality (p. 826).
**D. Thermal energy primarily warming skin and subcutaneous tissue.** Wrong, primarily warming the skin and subcutaneous tissue characterizes superficial modalities rather than ultrasound (p. 826).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 826.

q: A 68-year-old woman has vulvar itching, white plaques, and changes in labial architecture. Biopsy confirms lichen sclerosus. Which symptom-control treatment is described in Hazzard?
o: A moderate-strength topical glucocorticoid, followed by less frequent application
A topical estrogen preparation, followed by less frequent application
Observation without local treatment while no malignancy has been diagnosed
Observation without local treatment while no ulceration has developed
explanation:
**Symptomatic lichen sclerosus** is treated to control symptoms. Hazzard describes moderate-strength topical glucocorticoids followed by tapering application frequency; estrogen has little or no effect on the disease itself (p. 532).
"Treatment is necessary only to control symptoms." (p. 532).
"Typical regimens involve moderate strength topical glucocorticoids for at least 4 weeks, then tapering to a lower dosing frequency." (p. 532).

**A. A moderate-strength topical glucocorticoid, followed by less frequent application.** Correct, this matches the regimen described for symptom control in the cited chapter (p. 532).
**B. A topical estrogen preparation, followed by less frequent application.** Wrong, the source states that estrogen has little or no effect on lichen sclerosus, although it may help unaffected areas (p. 532).
**C. Observation without local treatment while no malignancy has been diagnosed.** Wrong, the treatment indication described is symptom control; the itching in the stem supplies that reason without requiring malignancy (p. 532).
**D. Observation without local treatment while no ulceration has developed.** Wrong, the source bases treatment on symptoms, not on waiting for ulceration in a symptomatic patient (p. 532).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 532.

q: A 76-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer presents after a fall. He has had increasing back pain for a month and difficulty walking. Examination shows L2–L3 tenderness, bilateral leg weakness (4/5), and reduced reflexes. PSA has risen to 67 ng/mL despite androgen deprivation therapy. X-rays show osteoblastic lesions in several vertebrae. Which approach to possible spinal cord compression follows Hazzard?
o: Complete assessment for a pathologic fracture before arranging definitive spinal imaging
Arrange urgent definitive spinal imaging, preferably MRI or CT myelography
Repeat the neurologic examination before arranging imaging if the weakness improves
Assess systemic cancer-treatment changes before arranging definitive spinal imaging
explanation:
**Spinal cord compression** should be suspected in a man with prostate cancer and new back pain; neurologic symptoms need not appear first (p. 1416). Hazzard states, "A negative neurologic examination should not delay a definitive radiologic study" (p. 1416). The back pain and weakness in the stem therefore warrant prompt imaging rather than the proposed delays.

**A. Complete assessment for a pathologic fracture before arranging definitive spinal imaging.** Wrong, fracture assessment does not remove the source’s instruction to pursue definitive imaging when cord compression is suspected (p. 1416).
**B. Arrange urgent definitive spinal imaging, preferably MRI or CT myelography.** Correct, MRI or CT myelography is the preferred definitive study for suspected compression; the source warns against delaying it (p. 1416).
**C. Repeat the neurologic examination before arranging imaging if the weakness improves.** Wrong, even a negative neurologic examination should not delay imaging, so improvement in weakness would not justify this sequence (p. 1416).
**D. Assess systemic cancer-treatment changes before arranging definitive spinal imaging.** Wrong, systemic treatment planning does not address the immediate need to evaluate suspected compression described on this page (p. 1416).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1416.

q: A 79-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment on screening (MoCA 22/30) and hypertension attends follow-up. His daughter reports that he gets lost on familiar routes and missed two bill payments this month. Delayed recall is 4/5 and clock drawing is 0/3. Examination shows mild cogwheel rigidity. Blood pressure is 145/85 mm Hg, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, and eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m². He takes amlodipine 5 mg daily and aspirin 81 mg. Which step directly assesses performance across cognitive domains to clarify the type and extent of impairment?
o: Begin donepezil treatment before characterizing the cognitive profile
Obtain formal neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile
Begin memantine treatment before characterizing the cognitive profile
Replace cognitive testing with contrast-enhanced structural brain imaging
explanation:
**Neuropsychological assessment** samples multiple cognitive domains and interprets the pattern alongside the history and medical evaluation (p. 867). Hazzard states: "patients are given tests that sample a variety of domains of cognitive function" (p. 867). That is the assessment requested here; brief screening does not by itself supply a comprehensive understanding of memory impairment (p. 867).

**A. Begin donepezil treatment before characterizing the cognitive profile.** Wrong, starting a symptomatic dementia treatment does not supply the domain testing requested. Hazzard chiefly recommends acetylcholinesterase inhibitors for patients already diagnosed with dementia; the current task is to characterize the impairment (pp. 867, 911).
**B. Obtain formal neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile.** Correct, formal testing samples cognitive domains and compares results with normative and estimated premorbid abilities, helping clarify dementia type and stage (p. 867).
**C. Begin memantine treatment before characterizing the cognitive profile.** Wrong, the source describes memantine for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease. Neither that diagnosis nor that stage is established here, and medication initiation does not perform the requested domain assessment (pp. 867, 911).
**D. Replace cognitive testing with contrast-enhanced structural brain imaging.** Wrong, the requested information is performance on cognitive tasks. Replacing those tests with structural imaging omits the domain sampling described by the source; this does not argue against imaging as another part of an evaluation (inference from p. 867).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 867, 911.

q: מה המשפט המתאר בצורה נכונה את הטיפול בהתקף GOUT בקשישים?
o: טיפול בסטרואידים בפוליארטיקולר גאוט ניתן ל-5-10 ימים עם ירידה הדרגתית (tapering)
טיפול ב- colchicine ניתן במינון 0.5 מ"ג 4 פעמים ביום ומופחת במקרה של שלשול
febuxostat ( פבוריק) עדיפה על allopurinol בחולה עם מחלת לב איסכמית
NSADIS לא סלקטיביים הוכחו כיעילים יותר מ- NSAIDS סלקטיביים בטיפול בגאוט
explanation:
For an acute gout flare, **anti-inflammatory treatment** is selected according to comorbidities, joint involvement and feasible administration. Low-dose colchicine, NSAIDs and corticosteroids are accepted options; age alone does not replace an individualized benefit–risk assessment (ACR 2020, Gout flare management).

**A. Corticosteroids for polyarticular gout for 5–10 days with tapering.** Correct, according to the official key. Oral corticosteroids are suitable when joint injection is impractical. The guideline distinguishes a course stopped directly from a short course followed by tapering; these schedules are not identical to the option's compressed wording (ACR 2012, Corticosteroids).
**B. Colchicine 0.5 mg four times daily, reduced if diarrhea occurs.** Wrong, low-dose treatment is preferred because efficacy is similar with fewer adverse effects. Kidney function and interactions require dose planning rather than waiting for diarrhea to guide dosing (ACR 2020, Gout flare management; ACR 2012, Colchicine).
**C. Febuxostat is preferable to allopurinol with ischemic heart disease.** Wrong, the guideline conditionally recommends considering an alternative to febuxostat in patients with cardiovascular disease, so ischemic disease is not a reason to prefer it (ACR 2020, Febuxostat).
**D. Nonselective NSAIDs are more effective than selective NSAIDs.** Wrong, COX-2 inhibitors are also effective; the guideline gives no blanket preference for a particular NSAID. Contraindications and tolerability guide selection (ACR 2012, NSAIDs).

Note: The official steroid option combines two separately presented regimens. It must not be interpreted as requiring tapering after every short course (ACR 2012, Corticosteroids).

Source: Khanna et al. 2012 ACR Guidelines for Management of Gout, Part 2. Arthritis Care Res. 2012;64:1447–1461, NSAIDs, Colchicine and Corticosteroids sections, doi:10.1002/acr.21773; FitzGerald et al. 2020 ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout. Arthritis Care Res. 2020;72:744–760, Febuxostat and Gout flare management, doi:10.1002/acr.24180.

q: באיזה מהבאים מתואר שילוב נכון של סוג הדמנציה והפרזנטציה הקלינית השכיחה?
o: דמנציה וסקולרית – תסמינים קוגניטיביים פלוקטואטיביים עם פגיעה בקשב
דמנציה עם גופיפי לוי (LBD) – ירידה קוגניטיבית אקוטית בעיקר בזיכרון קצר טווח
אלצהיימר – פגיעה בזיכרון ארוך טווח וחסרים נוירולוגיים פוקליים
דמנציה פרונטו-טמפורלית (FTD) – הפרעה בשפה עם זיכרון שמור יחסית
explanation:
**Frontotemporal dementia (FTD)** can present with early behavioral change or prominent language impairment and relative preservation of memory. The combination in the question fits the language presentation; it does not mean that all FTD begins with language impairment (p. 908, Table 59-5).

**A. Vascular dementia: fluctuating cognition with impaired attention.** Wrong, the table emphasizes fluctuations in cognition, attention and alertness in dementia with Lewy bodies. Its vascular-dementia course is linked to vascular events, stabilization or stepwise deterioration (p. 908).
**B. Dementia with Lewy bodies: acute cognitive decline mainly affecting short-term memory.** Wrong, the table describes progressive decline with fluctuations in attention and alertness, rather than this acute, predominantly short-term-memory presentation (p. 908).
**C. Alzheimer disease: impaired long-term memory and focal neurological deficits.** Wrong, AD is described as insidious and progressive, with prominent memory impairment; this combination of focal deficits and specifically long-term-memory loss is not its typical presentation in the table (p. 908).
**D. FTD: language impairment with relatively preserved memory.** Correct, early prominent language impairment with relative memory preservation fits the language presentation described in the table (p. 908).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 908.

q: במי מהמטופלים הבאים יש מקום לטיפול במעכבי CHOLIESTERASE?
o: מטופל עם תלונות על ירידה בזיכרון, MMSE 24/30, ללא שינוי בתפקודו או באורחות חייו
מטופל הסובל מ- DEMENTIA WITH LEWY BODIES, בדיקת MMSE אחרונה 10/30. כעת עם החמרת הלוצינציות ראיה טורדניות
מטופל עם דמנציה על רקע מחלת אלצהיימר, MMSE 8/30
מטופל עם FRONTOTEMPORAL DEMENTIA, בדיקת MMSE 22/30, כעת עם החמרה בדיסאינהיביציות
explanation:
A trial of a **cholinesterase inhibitor** is recommended in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and hallucinations may improve. Table 59-7 also includes donepezil for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease. In frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), there is no theoretical basis for these drugs and they may worsen agitation (Hazzard 8e, pp. 984, 912, 991).

**A. Memory complaints, MMSE 24/30, without a change in function or lifestyle.** Wrong, a complaint and screening score alone do not establish dementia warranting treatment. Preserved function can also fit mild cognitive impairment; this is an inference from the diagnostic distinction and treatment indications (pp. 869, 912).
**B. DLB, MMSE 10/30, with worsening distressing visual hallucinations.** Correct, the book recommends a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor in DLB and describes reduction or elimination of hallucinations, matching the troubling symptom in this case (p. 984).
**C. Alzheimer dementia, MMSE 8/30.** Correct, severe disease does not exclude the indication: donepezil is also listed for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease. This option was officially accepted (p. 912).
**D. Frontotemporal dementia, MMSE 22/30, with worsening disinhibition.** Wrong, there is no theoretical basis for cholinesterase inhibitors in FTLD, and they may aggravate agitation; disinhibition is not a reason to apply Alzheimer treatment to this disorder (p. 991).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 869, 912, 984, 991.
